draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

blocks.heading: Evidence
blocks.content: I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk, which is why I need the memo to distinguish what the data actually shows from what it cannot. The pilot recorded 160 boardings in week A and 240 boardings in week B [@lyra:1]. These figures count trips, not unique people [@lyra:1]. Because no attendance data were collected, an increase in boardings does not establish that more students came to class [@lyra:1]. The weeks differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized, so the observed increase reflects usage frequency rather than a causal change in attendance [@lyra:1]. This limits what we can infer from the raw usage data.

blocks.heading: Evidence
blocks.content: The survey compounds these gaps. Eighteen voluntary responses came from shuttle riders, but non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. Because the sample is voluntary and excludes those who do not use the service, the responses describe only these specific respondents and cannot establish demand across all students [@lyra:2]. Without random assignment or non-rider input, the data suggests rider preference, not campus-wide need.

live_draft_suggestions.base_content:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk, which is why I need the memo to distinguish what the data actually shows from what it cannot. The pilot recorded 160 boardings in week A and 240 boardings in week B [@lyra:1]. These figures count trips, not unique people [@lyra:1]. Because no attendance data were collected, an increase in boardings does not establish that more students came to class [@lyra:1]. The weeks differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized, so the observed increase reflects usage frequency rather than a causal change in attendance [@lyra:1]. This limits what we can infer from the raw usage data.
